comments.text:
# Resolution — 2026-09-10

**It is a torch, and as an object it is nothing at all.** The party carries a lit torch; the LIGHT
clock is how far it has burned; there is no `Lantern` record, no new fold entry, and no second
write path. What crosses the wire is a closed five-value level. What is on screen is a pool of
light owned by `World` and a mesh in the Knight's left hand.

The charting decision said "a carried lantern". That was an asset sighting, not a decision, and
four things found this session all point the other way.

---

# It is a torch, not a lantern

**§9 already calls it a torch.** `docs/ai-dm-system-design.md:612`, in the paragraph that
introduces this whole mechanism: *"The DM narrates what the table produced; it never decides that
the torch went out."* The design doc's own sentence for the thing names it.

**A torch is not lantern fuel.** §9's `Consumable` enum is potion / torch / rope, and
`emberdelve-ffi.6` made the torch the thing that resets the LIGHT clock. Feeding a torch into a
lantern is fictionally incoherent, and the DM narrates whatever the engine hands it — this is the
copper key with the polarity reversed, an engine fact the prose cannot honestly carry. The only
repair would be renaming the consumable to `oil`, against §9's written enum and three build
tickets.

**The kit already ships the handheld pair.** `godot/world/kits/kaykit_dungeon/torch.gltf` and
`torch_lit.gltf` — unlit and lit, distinct from the `torch_mounted` bracket `room.gd:352` puts on
walls. Going out is a mesh swap that already exists in the pack. `kaykit_halloween`'s
`lantern_standing`, which charting cited, is a *standing* lantern: floor dressing, not something a
figure holds.

**The Knight's hands are free and slotted.** `Knight.glb` has `handslot.l` and `handslot.r` as skin
joints — 2 of its 23 — and every stolen clip animates all 23, `Melee_1H_Attack_Chop` and `Death_A`
included. Its mesh list is nine body parts (`Knight_ArmLeft` … `Knight_Helmet`) with **no weapon**.
KayKit's intended attach point is empty and waiting, and a `BoneAttachment3D` there follows the
animation exactly.

**The cost, accepted:** a third use of the word. The party's `torch` consumable, the room's wall
fixtures, and now the thing in the hand. That is the `DIM` collision again — see
`Which clock moves a room's fires` — and it gets fixed the same way, in the glossary, with **wall
torch** reserved for the room's fixture and **carried torch** for the party's. `CONTEXT.md` is
amended in this session.

---

# As an object it is nothing new

**Rejected: it is a `Prop`.** Dead on inspection, and worth writing down so nobody re-proposes it.
`Prop` carries `x, y` in a room and ships inside `RoomView.props`; `Diff` has no `PropMoved`, so a
thing that moves every turn has no way to reach the client; `PropType`'s own comment says *"the
tileset defines the enum — the model can never name a prop that has no mesh"*, which is a statement
about room furniture; and `reveal_prop`'s closed per-room id enum would start including a thing
that is not in the room.

**The party's light is a pure function of the LIGHT clock.** No new event, no new field on
`PartyMember`, nothing added to the fold. The clock is already folded state under invariant 8, and
deriving the light from it means there is exactly one thing to keep correct. A replayed session
renders identically because the clock replays identically.

---

# What crosses the wire

A closed enum on `SceneState`, and a `Diff` for when it changes mid-turn:

| `PartyLight` | LIGHT segments (of 6) |
|---|---|
| `FULL` | 0–1 |
| `LOW` | 2–3 |
| `GUTTERING` | 4 |
| `FAILING` | 5 |
| `OUT` | 6 |

**The five names are not invented.** They are `What is on the LIGHT and ALERT tables`' own sign
names — `LIGHT_LOW` at segment 2, `LIGHT_GUTTERING` at 4, `LIGHT_FAILING` at 5, and `LIGHT_OUT` on
the fill. **What the DM narrates and what the player sees become the same five words.**

**The level is level-triggered; the signs stay edge-triggered.** A sign fires on crossing upward
only and re-arms on the way down (`ffi.2`). The level is read from the current segment count, so
spending a torch at `FAILING` puts the pool straight back to `FULL` and fires nothing on the way
down. Two rules, deliberately different, because a sign is an announcement and a level is a state.

**Rejected: ship the segment count.** Better that the wire *cannot* carry the counter than that the
client is trusted not to draw it. The map is explicit that the clock is diegetic and unlabelled and
that the shrinking pool is its whole read; shipping `filled: 4` hands the client the thing that must
never be on screen.

**Rejected: ship a radius in world units.** That puts an appearance number in Java, so
`How the shrinking light radius reads` would tune a look by recompiling the server. The client
already owns every number of that kind — `TORCH_ENERGY`, `TORCH_RANGE`, `UNLIT_TINT`, the ambient
`emberdelve-27l` just moved. What has to be server-owned is *how much light there is*, because that
folds from the log and must replay; metres are not that.

**The line for later.** If `How the shrinking light radius reads` gives the pool mechanical teeth —
less visible floor meaning less clickable floor — the server ships a **square list** alongside, the
way `SceneState.blocked` and `CombatView.legalMoves` already are. It does not turn the level into a
number. Invariant 1 is about decisions, not about pixels.

---

# Where the nodes live — split them

Three facts constrain this, and they rule out the obvious answer.

- `MAX_TORCH_LIGHTS` is deliberately a **per-`Room` budget** (`room.gd:313`). A light parented under
  a `Room` spends it, and the carried light must not.
- `world.gd:277` `_rebuild_tokens()` **frees and rebuilds every token on a room change**. A light
  parented to a token is destroyed and recreated on every crossing.
- Invariant 2. The light is the **party's**, not a member's. "Who is carrying the torch" is
  inventory-shaped and §16 defers it.

And the hand bone cuts both ways: `handslot.l` is animated by every clip, so anything attached there
swings with the chop. That is right for the mesh and wrong for the pool — a light pool that lurches
with a sword stroke is a lantern-swing effect nobody asked for.

**The light:** one `OmniLight3D` owned by `World`, a sibling of `Tokens`, positioned each frame at
the centroid of living player-controlled tokens. Exact rather than lagged, because `token.position`
is tweened in the same frame and `world.gd:40` already runs `_process`. It survives crossings, it
spends no room's budget, and at party size one it is simply over the fighter without any code
knowing that.

**The mesh:** a `torch` / `torch_lit` instance on a `BoneAttachment3D` at `handslot.l`, added
**after** `_fit()` and `_self_lit()` have run — otherwise it perturbs the bounding box the figure's
height calibration is measured from, and gets its materials rewritten by the emissive walk.

**Timeboxed.** The pool is the read; the mesh is garnish. If the mesh costs more than an hour it
comes out, because AGENTS.md names lighting as the single largest time sink in the project.

---

# The mesh across the cycle

**The party walks in holding a lit torch.** Not a decision — `emberdelve-ffi.6`'s arithmetic
already says so. LIGHT is 6 segments, the party starts with 2 torches, and the delve's light budget
is 18 ticks: 6 + 6 + 6. The clock starts empty and one torch is already burning.

**At `OUT` the mesh swaps, it never comes off.** `torch_lit` from `FULL` through `FAILING`, `torch`
at `OUT`. A hand that empties reads as the torch being dropped, which is a thing that did not
happen, and the board showing something the fiction never said is this project's characteristic
bug. The kit ships both meshes for exactly this.

The mesh is **two states**. Everything continuous — flame scale, flicker rate, whether the head dims
as it gutters — belongs to `How the shrinking light radius reads`.

---

# Out with none left

`OUT` with two torches in the pack and `OUT` with none look identical and mean opposite things: one
is a decision you reverse this turn, the other is the delve's failure spiral.

**No sixth enum value.** `PartyLight` describes light; the count describes supply, and fusing them
is the error `The numbers` named when it separated *where the doubt window sits* from *how much bar
is above it*. Both readers can already tell them apart: the player reads the count off the button,
greyed at zero; the DM reads it off the projection, since `What the projection carries` put all
three consumable counts there.

**One string changes.** `LIGHT_OUT`'s directive register takes a second clause when the count is
zero — *your last torch* rather than *your torch* — chosen server-side from state that already
exists. No new field, no new value.

---

# Never a pick target — and what replaces it

**The carried torch is never in `_target_under`.** Two rules say so and they agree.
`ADR-0011` — visible is not addressable. And `emberdelve-7m6`'s measured lesson: the picker was
confined because `brazier-east` stood between the camera corner and the north wall, won the ray, had
no intent to offer, and fell through to a null square, so the click did nothing and the failure was
silent. **A thing with nothing behind it must not shadow a thing that has something behind it.** A
mesh mounted at hand height on the party token is that object, in front of the camera, moving every
turn.

But the ticket's framing — *"a lantern the player can click is a lantern they can put down"* — hid
the real question. At `OUT`, in a dark room, spending a torch is the most consequential action in the
delve, and the only route to it would be typing something the mechanics model has to turn into
`use_item`. AGENTS.md names that exact class as the load-bearing risk in the architecture.

**So the torch gets a button, and so do the potion and the rest.**

---

# The exploration bar

The principle, which is the door's and is already structural in `net.gd`: **a button per player
action the DM does not adjudicate.** `moveTo`, `enterExit`, `attack` and `endTurn` are typed client
messages that reach the engine with no model in the path, because none of them is a question the DM
answers. A torch reset, a fixed 8-point potion and a fixed 4-point rest are the same shape. *Clicking
a door and walking through is the honest path*, and so is drinking a potion you already own.

This **amends** `Consumables as a counter map`' "no UI beyond a count" rather than punching through
it. The anti-goal there is *inventory* — "an item pipeline, a screen, and an enum that grows
forever" — and a button per entry of a closed enum §16 has already frozen cannot grow.

**Rejected: the button replaces the tool.** The player will type *"I drink a potion"* whatever
buttons exist, and a DM that narrates drinking one while nothing happens is the hotdog with a
healing potion in it. `use_item` stays in the mechanics set, and the button is a second path to the
same event — exactly as `enterExit` coexists with `use_exit`.

**Where it lives.** A sibling of `combat_bar.gd`, which is already the combat action bar; this is
its exploration counterpart. Not an extension of `party_badge.gd` — that node is
`MOUSE_FILTER_IGNORE` throughout and its own comment says it holds no facts, so making it clickable
inverts what it is. Every button keys off `Table.awaiting_dm`, the lock `debug_bar.gd:41` and
`combat_bar.gd:255` already use, so they go dead while the DM is speaking like everything else.

## Exploration-only, and that is a finding rather than a scope call

`docs/evidence/m4-attrition-sim.py:60` — `fight()` is *"one fight to the death — exits are illegal in
combat, so nobody leaves"* and it heals nobody. Every rest and potion in `delve()` happens between
rooms, at lines 112–116.

So `The numbers`' **45.7% survival at exactly 5 hit points** was measured with **no in-combat healing
in it**. A mid-fight potion does not merely need an action-economy rule §6 defers and the anti-goal
forbids — it invalidates the tuning that made §9's gate sentence arithmetically true. All three
buttons are exploration-only.

## The gates

**Rest.** The server refuses; the button greys as a hint. That is `SceneState.blocked`'s own stated
rule: *"The server refuses the move either way; this is the hint, not the rule."* And the gate is
**not** `mode == EXPLORATION` — `ffi.2`'s `Disposition.WARY` puts a living hostile on the board in
exploration mode, and you cannot rest while it watches you. The client reads living hostiles from
`Table.scene.entities`, which is already shipped and already current-room-scoped.

**Torch.** Refused only at **exactly zero segments**, where it would reset nothing. Spending at
`LOW` wastes two segments and stays legal, because that *is* the greed decision. This is
`Which clock moves a room's fires`' filter-at-draw rule one level up: an action offered that
provably does nothing is a lie in the UI, and using it would log a `use_item` that changed nothing.

---

# The directive rail is single-slot, and about to have five writers

`DmService.java:114` is **`private String pendingArrival`** — one slot. `noteCrossing` writes it
(`:948`), `takePendingArrival` clears it (`:952`), and only a free-text prose phase consumes it.

Writers it is about to have: the arrival line that exists today, LIGHT's signs at segments 2, 4 and
5, ALERT's signs, the room-fire move directive from `Which clock moves a room's fires`, and now a
torch relight. **Last write wins, silently.** A sign that gets overwritten is a clock that went
quiet — the exact failure `What is on the LIGHT and ALERT tables` built a sign table to prevent, and
it would present as the DM losing interest rather than as a bug.

Being straight about provenance: **the stale-directive half was already on the tracker.**
`emberdelve-xgg.12` recorded a stale *"you have come back"* directive landing **16 seconds later on a
key-searching turn**, after two rapid crossings. What this session adds is that the slot is about to
have five writers instead of one, which turns a P4 annoyance into a dropped sign.

**The rail becomes an ordered list, drained in order.** Filed against
`The Clock primitive, at DELVE scale` (`emberdelve-4h9.3`), which is where signs are built and which
already carries this map's amendments.

**A torch relight latches a directive.** One clause, no model call, consumed by the next prose phase.
Not because the player misses the moment — they can see the pool come back — but because the
projection will say the light is full again next turn with nothing to say why, and the narrator
reconciles that afresh every turn. That is what the 2026-09-07 playtest recorded about door state,
and what the player actually felt.

---

# Crossing narration reopens — as its own ticket

`emberdelve-4h9.12`'s notes settled that **every room entry ticks LIGHT, including a room already
visited**. So a LIGHT sign can fire *on a crossing*. With crossings silent, that sign sits on the
rail until the player's next typed turn, and the clock speaks late, attached to whatever they did
next.

Play judged the silence right in 2026-09-07 — 15 of 17 crossings produced no narration, and *"clicking
a door and walking through is the honest path"*. That judgement stands on its own terms. What
changed is that the rail now carries clock traffic, which did not exist when it was made.

The cost is measured and small: `Which clock moves a room's fires` puts a delve at ~9 room entries;
`openScene` runs 515–712ms to first token and 1.8–3.1s total; and a crossing already has cover — the
camera moves and a room draws. AGENTS.md: *"Speech latency is only expensive when nothing covers
it."* `emberdelve-xgg.12` even carries the sketch: a `narrateArrival(TurnSink)` modelled on
`openScene`, `takePendingArrival()` as the directive, `tryLock` rather than `lock`, one submit in
`enterExit`.

**Not decided here** — one ticket resolved per session, and turn structure for every crossing in the
game deserves its own resolution rather than a paragraph inside the torch ticket. Graduated as a new
map ticket, with `emberdelve-xgg.12` raised off P4 and pointed at it as the build. It belongs on this
map rather than under `xgg` because the argument that reopens it is an M4 argument.

---

# What was refused

- **A lantern.** §9 says torch, the kit ships a handheld torch pair, and a torch is not lantern fuel.
- **The light as a `Prop`.** No `PropMoved` diff, and `reveal_prop`'s enum would swallow it.
- **A new folded field for the light.** The clock is already the state; a second one is a second
  thing to keep correct.
- **The segment count on the wire.** The wire should be unable to carry the counter that must never
  be drawn.
- **A radius in world units on the wire.** Appearance numbers live on the client; the server owns
  how much light there is.
- **A sixth `PartyLight` value for "out with none left".** Light and supply are different axes.
- **The torch as a pick target.** `brazier-east`, at hand height, moving every turn.
- **The button replacing `use_item`.** The player will type it regardless, and a narrated potion that
  does nothing is the hotdog.
- **Potions in combat.** Not a taste call — the attrition tuning was measured without them.
- **A bone-attached light.** The mesh swings with the chop; the pool must not.
- **Deciding crossing narration here.** Graduated to its own ticket.

---

# What this changes downstream

- `The party carries a light` (`emberdelve-4h9.12`) — the whole object model.
- `Consumables as a counter map` (`emberdelve-4h9.2`) — the potion button, and the "no UI beyond a
  count" amendment.
- `The Clock primitive, at DELVE scale` (`emberdelve-4h9.3`) — the directive rail becomes an ordered
  list.
- `Rest — the pressure valve` (`emberdelve-4h9.11`) — the rest button and its hint-not-rule gate.
- `Props are not click targets yet` (`emberdelve-7m6`) — the carried torch is explicitly out.
- `How the shrinking light radius reads` (`emberdelve-ffi.5`) — unblocked, and it now has a named
  thing to shrink.
- `CONTEXT.md` — **carried torch**, **party light**, and **wall torch** as the disambiguation.

No ADR. This is an application of `ADR-0012`'s power budget and `ADR-0011`'s addressability rule, not
a new decision of that weight.

title: What is on the LIGHT and ALERT tables, and the signs under them
description:
## Question

What is on the LIGHT and ALERT consequence tables, and on the sign tables under them?

§9 makes the table the point, not an implementation detail: it is "the same constrain-the-model
pattern as the DC bands in §7 and the prop enum in §5. The DM narrates what the table produced; it
never decides that the torch went out." A clock with a vague table is a clock that hands the
decision back to the model.

## Two tables per clock, because clocks speak twice

Settled at charting: a **threshold** fires a sign, the **fill** fires the consequence. So each clock
needs both.

- **Signs** are §9's region-scale device brought down to delve scale: "spoor, smoke, tracks, rolled
  a watch ahead of the meeting itself. Gives the player a chance to avoid it and gives the narrator
  something to foreshadow, which is the cheapest available source of the thing generated content is
  usually worst at." A distant scrape, a door found open, the lantern flame leaning.
- **Consequences** are the state change. `LIGHT_OUT` is the obvious one on the light table. The
  alert table's entries are the ones with room to be interesting — and note that room torches
  guttering is legitimate *here*, as an engine-fired consequence, where it was ruled out as a DM
  tool.

## What has to be decided

- The entries themselves, on all four tables.
- Whether a consequence is drawn or fixed. §9 says "fires a table", which implies a draw, but a
  one-entry table is a fixed consequence and is allowed to be.
- What a consequence is allowed to *do*. `LIGHT_OUT` changes lighting state. May a consequence
  spawn? Move something? Tick another clock? Each of those is a different amount of machinery, and
  the anti-goal against building a rules engine applies.
- How a consequence reaches the client. It has to be an event and a diff like everything else
  (invariant 8), and the client renders what it is told (invariant 1).
- Whether the ALERT table can end in combat, given `start_combat` is currently a model decision and
  emberdelve-vy7 records that the model already escalates too eagerly. An engine-fired fight is
  arguably the *fix* for that, not a duplicate of it.

## Constraint

Closed enums, validated server-side (invariant 7). `ConsequenceId` is named in §9's record and is
the seam.
acceptance_criteria: Four tables written out: LIGHT consequences, LIGHT signs, ALERT consequences, ALERT signs. Every entry a closed ConsequenceId. A stated rule for what a consequence may do to the world, and whether ALERT may start a fight.
close_reason: Resolved: four tables written. A consequence may only do what a tool can already do; a sign is a consequence with an empty bundle. LIGHT fixed one-entry, ALERT drawn from four. Full answer in the resolution comment.

comments.text:
# Resolution — 2026-09-09

Four tables, written out below. The rule that made them writable is the **power budget**:

> **A consequence may only do what a tool can already do.**

A `ConsequenceId` is a named, pre-validated bundle of events the engine already has an
`Event` + `Diff` pair for — `EntitySpawned`, `EntityMoved`, `PropRevealed`, `CombatStarted` —
plus state the engine already models as a scalar (lighting, a clock's fill). No new verbs, no
effect language. §12's anti-goal against a rules engine is the reason, and §15 already puts the
effect interpreter with the content milestone; an effect language reached through the back door
of a consequence table is the same tax under a different name.

## The unification that made this smaller than expected

**A sign is a consequence whose bundle is empty.** Same record, same table, same directive
machinery, same firing path — the only difference is whether anything changes. That is what lets
the acceptance criterion ("every entry a closed `ConsequenceId`") be literally true rather than
aspirational, and it is why there is **one enum, not two**.

The cost, stated so it is not discovered later: nothing type-level stops a sign table from
holding `LIGHT_OUT`. That is a validation rule — a sign table's entries must have empty bundles —
rather than a type. Taken deliberately over a separate `SignId`, which would make the mistake
unrepresentable at the price of duplicating the directive machinery.

---

# LIGHT

The party's lantern. The player can see this clock; the shrinking radius **is** the read
(`emberdelve-ffi.5` owns how).

## Consequences — one entry, fixed

| `ConsequenceId` | Bundle | Directive register |
|---|---|---|
| `LIGHT_OUT` | Party light drops to its lowest level. ALERT +1, declared on the tick side. | The lantern has gone out. |

**One entry on purpose.** LIGHT being fully predictable is what makes the greed decision
*computable* — the player should be able to plan against the dark and count torches against
rooms. ALERT is the clock allowed to surprise you, and that asymmetry is most of what
distinguishes them. A one-entry table is a fixed consequence and is allowed to be.

The clock does not stop at full. It sits full until a `torch` is spent, which states the greed
loop in one line: how deep you go is how many torches you brought.

## Signs

| Segment (of 6) | `ConsequenceId` | What it is about |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | `LIGHT_LOW` | The ring of light has drawn in. |
| 4 | `LIGHT_GUTTERING` | The flame stutters; the shadows swing. |
| 5 | `LIGHT_FAILING` | Light at arm's length. One more and it is gone. |

Quiet for two segments, then every segment. That acceleration is the whole reason the sign table
is a map from segment to `ConsequenceId` rather than a single named threshold.

---

# ALERT

How much the site has noticed you. The player **cannot** see this clock — its entire read is its
signs, which is why it carries three of them and why its fill has variety.

## Consequences — drawn

| `ConsequenceId` | Bundle | Disposition |
|---|---|---|
| `PATROL_ARRIVES` | `EntitySpawned` in the party's room + `CombatStarted` | `HOSTILE` |
| `SOMETHING_WANDERS_IN` | `EntitySpawned` in the party's room | `WARY` |
| `THE_DARK_CLOSES_IN` | Room lighting drops one level | — |
| `DRAWN_BY_THE_NOISE` | `EntityMoved` — a hostile already in the site crosses into the party's room + `CombatStarted` | `HOSTILE` |

`DRAWN_BY_THE_NOISE` depends on `emberdelve-4h9.9`; until that lands the table draws from the
first three. It is carried because a site whose creatures **converge** is a better site than one
that spawns from nowhere, and entities already carry a `roomId` since schema v2, so it is
expressible without new machinery.

`THE_DARK_CLOSES_IN` is the entry the ticket explicitly sanctioned: room torches guttering is
legitimate *here*, as an engine-fired consequence, where it was ruled out as a DM tool. It is the
one entry with no mechanical bite, and it earns its place — a table that **always** spawns
something is a table the player reads as "a fight is coming" after two draws.

## Signs

| Segment (of 6) | `ConsequenceId` | What it is about |
|---|---|---|
| 2 | `SOMETHING_STIRRED` | Far off, something moved and went quiet. |
| 4 | `THE_FLAME_LEANS` | A draught, from somewhere that was shut. |
| 5 | `IT_IS_CLOSE` | Near enough to hear. It knows roughly where you are. |

`THE_FLAME_LEANS` reads the ALERT clock **through the lantern**. It ties the two clocks together
in the fiction without tying them together in the machinery, and it is the kind of foreshadowing
§9 names as the thing generated content is worst at producing on its own.

## The ALERT band vocabulary

`emberdelve-ffi.1` left this as a named slot for this ticket. Filled. In `## The party`,
alongside `lantern: guttering`:

```
the site: stirring
```

| Fill | Band |
|---|---|
| 0–1 | `quiet` |
| 2–3 | `stirring` |
| 4–5 | `hunting` |
| full | `on you` |

Bands, not a count, under ffi.1's rule: no tool takes the alert level as an argument, so the
number buys nothing and costs what AGENTS.md warns about — an invitation to read it aloud.

---

# The rules the tables needed

## What ticks what

The trap is that two clocks ticking on the same events are one clock with two faces. They share a
baseline and differ in what is extra.

| Trigger | LIGHT | ALERT |
|---|---|---|
| Room entered | +1 | +1 |
| Rest taken | +1 | +1 |
| Failed check | +1 (natural 1: +2) | — |
| A fight starts | — | +1 |
| LIGHT fills | — | +1 |

A fight is the noisiest thing in the game, and ticking ALERT on one puts a cost on combat that
combat does not currently have — it turns "fight it or avoid it" into a resource decision, which
is the greed loop's sibling, for free.

**LIGHT filling ticks ALERT, and it is declared on the tick side, not buried inside `LIGHT_OUT`.**
Going dark making you noisier is the spiral that gives a delve an endgame. Modelling it as a
cross-clock effect inside a consequence was considered and refused: a clock that ticks a clock is
the first step toward a state machine nobody can trace. It is a tick trigger. It stays legible.
This is also charting's "death follows from a filled light clock indirectly, which is enough."

## Discharge is asymmetric

**ALERT resets to empty when it fills. LIGHT stays full until a torch is spent.**

Not arbitrary: light is a quantity you *spend*, alert is a state that *discharges*. It is also
the only way ALERT can fire more than once in a delve, without which its table is a one-shot.

## Signs fire on crossing upward only, and re-arm on the way down

Without this, spending a torch to refuel LIGHT fires `LIGHT_GUTTERING` on the way back down — the
narrator announcing the light failing on the turn the player fixed it.

## Disposition — two values, not one

`Disposition { HOSTILE, WARY }`, with room for §9's full hostile-through-friendly band later.

**An ALERT consequence brings something in; it does not decide how the meeting goes.** Combat
follows from the disposition, not from the spawn.

`WARY` needs **no new machinery**: the creature is on the board, combat has not started, and if
the player swings, `start_combat` fires as a provoked fight. That is exactly the state the M2 and
M3 sessions already produced by accident (a goblin spawned, no combat started). It is §9's
"avoid the encounter" play for free, and it is `SOMETHING_WANDERS_IN`'s whole point.

A one-value enum was refused for the reason AGENTS.md records about capability flags: **a claim,
not a behaviour**. An unexercised seam is one that will be wrong the day a neutral NPC exists —
and the standing worry is precisely that a player should not kill an NPC they were not determined
to kill. This makes that structural rather than a prompt rule.

## What the log says

`ConsequenceFired` **plus** the bundled events. Inert in the fold, carried for the record.

Refused hardest: a `ConsequenceFired` that the fold expands via the tables. That would make a
content file part of replay correctness — edit a table after a session is recorded and it
silently replays differently. Same argument `Event.PartyMoved` already makes for carrying its
landing square rather than recomputing it from `Exit.inward()`.

Bundled-events-only was refused too: it loses the causal record, and this project's whole
diagnostic workflow is "the file that proves it is already on disk." A session where a fight
appeared from nowhere and the log cannot name the clock is a session you cannot diagnose. One
inert event is the price, and `ToolCallIssued` already pays exactly that price for exactly that
reason.

Two things this forces rather than chooses:

- **`ClockTicked` must be an event**, or a clock is not in the log and is not a fold (invariant 8).
- **It must carry the resulting fill** rather than have the fold count ticks — same argument as
  above.

The draw on a multi-entry table is logged **in `ConsequenceFired`**, not as a `RollResult`. It is
not a die the player watches, and `isDramatic()` would gate it out anyway.

## Which rail a sign rides

**The latched directive rail** — `pendingArrival`'s, not `narrateCombat`'s.

A sign is foreshadowing, not an event: nothing happened, something is *going to*. There is
nothing on screen to cover an interrupting prose call — the dice cover an exploration turn, the
animation covers a combat beat, a sign has neither — so an immediate call buys an empty screen,
which is the 2.5s row the project already misses. And a dropped sign is worse than a late one,
because the whole point is giving the player a chance to act on it.

**This makes signs free: they cost no extra model call at all.**

It is also less late than it first looks. Every tick trigger fires inside a player turn, and the
mechanics phase runs in front of the prose phase — so a failed-check tick's sign drains on **that
same turn's** prose call. Only a room-entry tick waits, because `WsHandler.enterExit` runs no
prose phase, and the 2026-09-07 playtest already judged a silent crossing to be right.

## Two directives, one turn

The arrival directive and a sign directive **both go**, sign appended to arrival.

Not an edge case: rooms entered ticks both clocks, so once the clocks are biting this is the
**normal** shape of an arrival. Dropping the sign there silences the clock at exactly the moment
it should speak. A queue was refused — the engine latches and every player turn drains, so more
than two cannot accumulate without a turn passing.

The cost is named because it is measured: AGENTS.md records that *writing more* made the model
more verbose, 514 → 654 characters. **A sign directive is one clause**, in `ARRIVAL_FIRST`'s
register — "The lantern has burned lower. Work it in." — never a paragraph about what the light
means.

## A sign that fires during combat is dropped

Combat is the one case where the latch would wait past usefulness — the next exploration turn
could be many rounds away. AGENTS.md's asymmetry rule already decides this: engine-generated
narration gives up rather than arriving late. The ALERT band stays in the projection continuously,
so the DM still knows; only the beat is lost. Riding the next combat beat was refused because
combat directives are deliberately terse and appending to them fights the one thing combat
narration has measured.

---

# What this decides for `emberdelve-vy7`

Taken here rather than deferred, because the ALERT table is what replaces it.

**`start_combat` stays, for provoked fights. `dm-tools.md`'s two-failure escalation rule goes.**
The engine's ALERT clock becomes the only source of an *unprovoked* fight.

A player who swings a sword needs a fight to start, so routing that through a clock is absurd;
what was wrong was never that the model could start a fight, but that it decided *unprovoked*
escalation by reading a fuzzy rule. Both 2026-09-07 sessions escalated on the **first** failure,
and one put the player in initiative before they had done anything hostile. That rule was not
producing tension, it was producing a coin flip — and it decides what kind of game the session is
on turn one.

**The behavioural change, named rather than left to be found in play:** ALERT does not tick on
failed checks. So a player who fails check after check in one room now generates no escalation at
all, where today they would get a fight. That is correct — failed checks still cost, in LIGHT,
which is the currency that does not ambush you — but it is a real change to a milestone that
passed its gate.

---

# New build work this surfaces

- **Room lighting has no `Diff`.** `RoomView` carries `LightingPreset lighting`, but nothing in
  the `Diff` union can change it after the scene is sent. `THE_DARK_CLOSES_IN` needs one.
- **`Disposition` on a spawn**, and the rule that combat follows from it.
- **`ClockTicked` and `ConsequenceFired`** events, and the schema bump they imply.

Filed against `emberdelve-4h9.3`, which owns the Clock primitive.

# Not decided here

- **Segment counts, and how hard a rest ticks** — `emberdelve-ffi.6`. The tables above are written
  against a working assumption of 6 segments; the thresholds are relative positions (quiet early,
  every segment late), and ffi.6 pins the integers.
- **What the shrinking radius looks like** — `emberdelve-ffi.5`.
- **What the lantern is as an object** — `emberdelve-ffi.3`.

title: A dev-only room preview and prop-placing tool in the Godot editor
description:
Placing props by typing x/y into room JSON, restarting the server and walking to the room
is the loop that authoring 4-5 rooms with 20+ props each would run several hundred times.
A dev-only Godot editor tool collapses it: load a room, see it with the real meshes, drag
a prop to a square, write the position back.

It also happens to be where the appearance work in 4h9.7 gets done. Choosing which of
eleven container meshes reads right in a torchlit crypt is a judgement made by looking,
and in the tool it is a dropdown rather than an edit-restart-walk cycle.

WHAT MAKES THIS CHEAP HERE

room.gd contains no reference to Table - its own docstring says so, "this node reads
nothing from Table, so both go through one build path". And room.gd:554 _to_world already
falls back to a self-centred grid when there is no World ancestor. A Room node standing
alone in an editor scene builds itself correctly. That fallback exists for another reason
(an unregistered room draws on the entrance rather than at NaN) but it is what makes the
preview a small script rather than a port.

Room.build reads eight keys: roomId, width, height, floorType, wallType, lighting, exits,
coveredWalls, plus visited via level_for.

Props are not built by Room. world.gd:236 _instance_prop does it, reading id, hidden,
type, x, y, rotation, and calling configure(prop, room_id) - which mesh_prop.gd:32 does
without touching Table either. So props are editor-safe too.

TWO RULES THAT DECIDE WHETHER THIS IS AN ASSET OR A LIABILITY

Extract the prop instancing into one shared function that world.gd and the tool both
call. Do not copy it. _rebuild_rooms already makes this argument about rooms: "One build
path for all of them (Room.build), so the wall rule cannot come out differently on either
side of a door." The tool is a third caller. A preview that builds props its own way is a
preview that lies.

Round-trip the whole JSON file on write. Parse it, mutate only the x, y and rotation of
the prop that moved, re-serialize. Never rebuild the file from the fields the tool knows
about - that silently drops description, contains, hidden and revealHint, and the loss
does not show up until a session plays wrong.

THE SOURCE OF TRUTH DOES NOT MOVE

Room JSON stays the definition; the tool is an editor for it and never a second place a
room is defined. Same reasoning as invariant 8, applied to content instead of state.

For a single room the content shape is close enough to the wire shape to read directly:
crypt.json already carries roomId, width, height, floorType, wallType, lighting, props
and exits at the top level, and its exits already carry x, y and direction. Add
visited=true and coveredWalls=[] and Room.build accepts it - and for a lone room the empty
coveredWalls is correct rather than a shortcut, per scene_fixtures.gd: "A lone room is
nearest the entrance by definition and so covers nothing."

That stops being true the moment you want to preview two rooms side by side, because
coveredWalls is then a real answer only Rooms.coveredWalls() can give. At that point add a
server flag - dump the actual RoomView JSON next to what RoomDumper already writes - and
have the tool eat the wire shape. Do not reimplement coveredWalls in GDScript; it took
three attempts server-side and the failures were holes in walls.

PATHS

Room JSON lives at server/src/main/resources/content/rooms/, outside res:// (which is
godot/). Reach it with ProjectSettings.globalize_path("res://") plus a relative hop, not a
hardcoded absolute path and not a symlink, so it survives the repo being cloned elsewhere.
Gradle copies resources at build; a running server picks up an edit on restart.
acceptance_criteria:
A dev-only editor tool loads a room from its JSON, renders it with the real kit meshes and
the game's own build path, and writes a moved prop's x, y and rotation back to the source
file with every other field preserved byte for byte. Prop instancing is one function that
the game and the tool share. Nothing in the tool is on the shipped path.
notes:
SPIKE RUN 2026-09-07, and what it settled. godot/dev/preview_room.gd is on disk and works:
the crypt draws in the editor viewport with the real kit meshes - 144 floor, 48 walls,
16 torches, 7 of 8 props, the eighth being door-north (DOOR), which is correct because
the door is the wall segment. It is a prototype, not this issue's deliverable: read-only,
single-room, and carrying three copies of code the real tool must share instead.

THE RULE THE SPIKE COST FOUR ROUND TRIPS TO LEARN

A non-@tool script is a PLACEHOLDER INSTANCE in the editor. It keeps its exported values
and loses every method. So anything editor tooling needs to CALL needs @tool; anything it
merely instantiates from code (Room) does not. The symptom is always the same line -
"Attempt to call a method on a placeholder instance" - and it is worth recognising on
sight, because it names the wrong file: it names the caller.

Now @tool, and all four are permanent rather than spike-only:

  world/prop_table.gd     - scene_for() could not be called, so no prop drew at all
  world/props/mesh_prop.gd - configure() builds PILLAR and RUBBLE meshes at runtime
  world/props/sarcophagus.gd - _ready() mounts the lid skull
  world/props/alcove.gd   - _ready() positions the recess pieces

The last two carry an _editing_myself() guard and need it. Their _ready writes to
transforms that belong to the .tscn, so a bare @tool would bake computed positions into
the authored file the next time someone opened and saved alcove.tscn. The guard is
`Engine.is_editor_hint() and get_tree().edited_scene_root == self` - skip when this node
IS the scene being edited, run when it is an instance built somewhere else, which is all
the preview ever makes.

world/world.gd MUST NOT get @tool. Its _ready connects to the Table autoload, so an
editor-resident World is a live websocket client inside the editor. Everything the tool
wants from World - grid_to_world, room_origin - has to come from somewhere else.

TWO TRAPS WITH NO ERROR MESSAGE BETWEEN THEM

Adding @tool to a script does not take effect in a running editor. The placeholder stays
loaded and the same error repeats, which reads exactly like the edit not working.
Project > Reload Current Project after any @tool change.

Do not open world.tscn to host the preview. Its root IS a World, Room._host_world walks
up the tree and finds it, and every call through it fails on the placeholder
(room.gd:551 room_origin, room.gd:558 grid_to_world). preview_room.gd now refuses that
case by name. A blank 3D scene plus its own WorldEnvironment is the arrangement that
works.

ONE MORE FOR WHOEVER IS LOOKING AT PROPS

The editor's Preview Sun and Preview Environment toggles are on by default and stack on
top of whatever environment the tool adds, so the room reads far brighter than the game.
Turn both off before judging how a mesh looks, or every appearance decision in 4h9.7 gets
made under the wrong light.

WHAT THE REAL TOOL STILL HAS TO DO

Write back (the whole point, and absent). Share the prop instancing with world.gd instead
of copying it. Share grid_to_world instead of copying it. Read the environment off
world.tscn instead of restating its four numbers. Handle more than one room, which is
where the --dump-view server flag becomes necessary because coveredWalls stops being [].
Pick the room from a list rather than a const you edit and re-run.

Unrelated and pre-existing, so nobody chases it twice: the three "Unicode parsing error /
Unexpected NUL character" lines at editor startup are addons/gut/source_code_pro.fnt, a
binary bitmap font Godot tries to read as UTF-8. Committed in 47fae7f, untouched. Every
text file in the project is clean UTF-8 with no NUL bytes.

title: Combat verbs and initiative live in the frame, only during a fight
description:
combat_bar.gd is a 42px strip pinned to the top of the overlay. Relocate its
contents into the frame: initiative chips along the top of the playfield (over
the world, like the party badge), and Attack / Move / End Turn in the chin,
right of the log.

These exist only while Table.mode is COMBAT (and while the existing bar would
have been visible, including the dissolve). Exploration has no chips and no
verbs; the log takes the chin width.

End Turn keeps Net.end_turn(activeId). Attack and Move do not grow new click
modes — they are visible verbs for click-the-board, dimmed from
actionAvailable / movementRemaining the way the current bar already does.

Reuse combat_bar.gd timing (arrival(), CHIP_* constants, backdating from
opened_at) so a mid-fight reconnect does not replay the drums. Layout changes;
the ceremony does not.
design:
The 42px CombatBar Control can move or the script can be hung on new nodes in
the frame. Do not duplicate the fold of CombatView. Debug → start combat is
the play path.

The old top strip going away is the point: mode is legible from whether chips
and verbs exist, not from a bar across the sky.
acceptance_criteria:
- Exploration: no initiative chips, no Attack/Move/End Turn.
- Debug → start combat: chips appear over the playfield, verbs appear in the chin, End Turn still ends the turn.
- Movement remaining and action available still gate the verbs from the server's CombatView.
- Arrival timing still uses opened_at / arrival() so a reconnect does not restage the ceremony.
- Existing combat_bar tests updated for the new nodes and still pass.
close_reason: Chips over the playfield, Attack/Move/End Turn in the chin, only during a fight (including dissolve). CombatView still gates the verbs; arrival() timing unchanged; End Turn still Net.end_turn.

title: Dramatic rolls take the chin as a free-standing die
description:
dice_tray.gd is a bottom-right overlay Control drawing tumble.gd samples. Move
that presentation into the chin's right side. The die is free-standing — no
inner tray well, no recessed pit. Stakes, arithmetic, and outcome sit around it
(ATHLETICS CHECK · DC 20, 14 + 3 = 17, HIT/SUCCESS) the way the tray already
does from the first frame.

Visible only while a dramatic roll is in flight (Tumble.is_dramatic: attacks,
checks, saves). Damage and initiative stay log-only. When nothing is in flight
the chin-right is empty (or occupied only by combat verbs if a fight is open).

A check during exploration shows the die without Attack/Move/End Turn. An
attack during combat can show the die next to the verbs. No full-screen check
overlay in this task.

tumble.gd stays pure and stays the only thing that decides where a sample is.
Clock.hold timing is unchanged. No click-to-throw.
design:
Keep DiceTray as overlay chrome, not a 3D object in World (test_chrome already
pins that). Re-anchor it into the chin. COMBAT_HOLD_MS, land_at, reveal_at,
IMPACT_BEAT_MS stay.

The log already records the same roll; the chin die is the ritual, the log is

- No die in the chin when no dramatic roll is in flight.
- debug → roll d20 (or a skill check) shows a free-standing d20 in the chin with stakes and 14 + 3 = 17-style arithmetic around it, not inside a tray well.
- Exploration check: die appears, combat verbs do not.

- tumble.gd is not rewritten. dice_tray and chrome tests pass.

title: Float the party badge over the playfield
description:
The party is not a left sidebar. A circular portrait floats over the top-left of
the playfield (over WorldView, not in its own stone column) so the crypt keeps

Mouse filter ignore on the badge so it cannot swallow a click meant for the

title: Inset WorldView in a stone frame and move the log into the chin
description:
WorldView currently fills the window (chrome.tscn) and Overlay/Log is a 42% veil
at the bottom-left. test_chrome.gd pins SubViewport size to the window and the

the camera centres on the window and the near edge of the room sits under the
