title: More than one hostile on the board
description:
"Several skeletons in one room." Today the board holds one goblin and GoblinAi runs it.

WHAT IS IN

More than one hostile alive at once, in initiative, each taking a turn. A second stat
block so a fight has composition rather than a stack of one thing - the Skeleton_Warrior
mesh is already the goblin's, so this is content and turn order, not art.

Authored spawns. M3 carried this forward: "Authored secrets still have no spawn.
Listening at the lid produced a durable fact and no goblin. theSarcophagus says Vessk is
in the box; spawn_entity is still a model decision. The hotdog class, now behind a door."
A room that says something is in the sarcophagus should be able to put it there without
the model choosing to.

WHAT IS OUT, AND THIS IS THE LINE THAT MATTERS

Not the effect interpreter. Not conditions, resistances, reach, cover, opportunity
attacks. Section 15 puts the SRD engine, the content and the stance layer in one
milestone together, after this one, because each is a tax alone: "an effect interpreter
with a single attack to interpret, or a stance call choosing between aggressive and
aggressive, is overhead."

N enemies against the existing forty lines of resolveAttack is the whole scope. If this
task starts modelling conditions, it has gone wrong.

Not the stance layer either. Section 16's re-entry condition is "a second monster kind
exists, so there is a choice to make and a fight can read as coordinated" - which this
task creates. Note it when it lands; do not build it here.

WATCH THE NARRATION BUDGET

One narration call per enemy turn, move and swing together, is the existing rule and it
exists to stop combat going to a five-second-per-click clock. With four hostiles that
rule is load-bearing rather than a nicety. AGENTS.md, Combat narration, and the open
"attacking during an enemy-turn narration drops the kill's narration" defect both get
worse with more enemies - decide whether the board locks or the beat queues before
finding out at four skeletons.

Initiative currently throws one roll at a time in the tray. Every combatant at once is
why initiative is not dramatic; check that holds at N.
acceptance_criteria:
A fight with at least three hostiles of two kinds resolves end to end with no model in
the path, under debug start combat. Room content can spawn a hostile without the model
calling spawn_entity. resolveAttack is unchanged in shape. One narration call per enemy
turn still holds, and a full enemy round stays inside the four-second budget.
notes:
**Stat blocks settled by emberdelve-ffi.6.**

- **The goblin is weakened: AC 12, HP 6, +3, 1d4+1** (from AC 15, HP 7, +4, 1d6+2).
- **The new block is a brute: AC 13, HP 16, +4, 1d8+2.**

**Why the goblin has to move, which was not obvious.** Against a party of one the action economy
inverts the intuitive ladder: N weak enemies is *always* harder than one strong enemy, because each
of them takes a full turn while the fighter takes one. At HP 12 today: one brute drops the fighter
23.7% of the time, two goblins 43.2%, three goblins 79.9%. So "a few weak mobs" cannot be the easy
fight while the goblin is AC 15 / HP 7 / 1d6+2. It has to become the mob it is already described as
-- `goblin.json` says "a wiry goblin scavenger, filthy with grave-dust" and gives it **AC 15**,
which is chain mail.

**HP 6 specifically.** The fighter's 1d8+3 has a minimum of 4, so at HP 4 or 5 the mob dies to
literally every hit that connects and a pack is a formality. HP 6 leaves it at 75% one-shot --
usually one blow, sometimes two.

**The brute is what meets §9's gate.** It puts the doubt window at **4-10, 50% at 6 hp, 45.7%
survival at exactly 5**, while dropping a full-health fighter only 8.2% of the time: a fight you
almost never lose fresh and genuinely might lose hurt. That is the sentence "stand in front of a
door at 5 hit points and genuinely not know" made arithmetically true.

**Build warning, and it is not a content-only edit.** `CombatEngineTest` constructs its fixture
through `new GameEngine(new ContentLoader(), ...)`, so it reads the real `fighter.json` and
`goblin.json`. Its scripted die faces are chosen against AC 15 and 7 hp and will all need reworking
-- e.g. `CombatEngineTest.java:350` asserts "12 hp less 4+2 damage". `WorldStateTest` and
`EventLogTest` construct `Entity` records directly and are unaffected.

**Recorded logs are unaffected.** `EntitySpawned` carries the whole `Entity`, so a replayed session
uses the stats it was written with. No schema bump, no `recordFixture`.

`AGENTS.md`'s shortcuts table Goblin row becomes untrue when this lands.

Numbers and method: `docs/evidence/m4-attrition-sim.py`.

title: Author the site - 4-5 rooms, an objective, a way out
description:
Retires the AGENTS.md anti-goal "do not add a third room". That was M3-scoped and it is
spent: two rooms cannot hold a decision about whether to push deeper.

Section 9, Bounded sites: "Sites are finite: a handful of rooms, an objective, an exit,
an ending. Quest-linked, scattered across the region, many of them. Not a hole that
generates downward forever."

SHAPE

Four or five rooms. An entrance that is also the way out. Two middles. A room holding
the objective, sitting shallow. Something worth taking that sits deeper than the
objective does - that is the greed decision, and section 9 calls it "tension for free,
inside a bounded space, with an ending".

The crypt and the gallery are the fixed points every M0 through M3 measurement was taken
in. Extend the site around them rather than replacing them, or the comparison is gone.

WHY THIS IS ALSO THE GENERATOR SPEC

M1's outstanding half comes after this epic, and the reason it comes after is that
nobody yet knows what a generated room has to contain. M3 carried the symptom forward:
"Generated rooms still have nothing to find. PropPlacer marks nothing hidden, so
reveal_prop is never offered."

Authoring the site answers it. Whatever these rooms need - a hidden prop, an encounter
slot, an objective anchor, a place for a clock to tick, a way out - is what
LayoutGenerator and PropPlacer have to be able to produce. Write that list down as it
emerges; it is the input to the next milestone.

TWO THINGS THE 2026-09-07 PLAYTEST SAYS TO GET RIGHT

Door descriptions must match what crossExit actually enforces. Both sessions invented an
ATHLETICS DC 20 to kick a door that was never shut, because every authored door said
"no handle on this side" while the engine refused nothing but leaving mid-fight. If a
door in this site is meant to be shut, it needs emberdelve-ql3 behind it. If it is not,
its description must not say so.

Put revealHints where a player will actually look. The gallery niche was never found in
either session - its hint is on the west wall and both players searched the brazier and
the pillars.
acceptance_criteria:
Four or five authored rooms forming one site with an entrance that is also the exit, an
objective placed shallow, and something worth more placed deeper. Every door description
agrees with what the engine enforces. A written list of what a room in this site must be
able to contain, as the generator milestone's input.
notes:
**Site shape settled by emberdelve-ffi.6: five rooms, about three holding a fight.**

The objective sits shallow, leaving two rooms of genuinely optional depth -- which is where the
greed decision lives at all.

**The encounter ladder**, against the settled fighter (HP 20) and the settled stat blocks
(emberdelve-4h9.9):

| Encounter | Dropped from full | 50% at | Doubt window |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2 mobs | 1.3% | 3 hp | 1-5 |
| 1 brute | 8.2% | 6 hp | 4-10 |
| 3 mobs | 12.0% | 9 hp | 8-13 |
| brute + 2 mobs | 52.7% | 20 hp | 18-20 |

One brute and three mobs land on comparable weight -- two shapes, one difficulty, which is the
variety the site wants without a cliff. **brute + 2 mobs is not a designed room**; it is what the
ALERT clock does to a party that let it fill.

Whole delves: careful (3 fights, objective, out) is lost **26.1%** of the time, leaving 10.8/20 hp
and 2.5 items; greedy (5 fights, two rooms deeper) is lost **77.1%**. The careful figure assumes
the player fights everything and avoids nothing -- avoidance is what the ALERT signs are for.

Interacts with a locked M2 decision worth restating here: **exits are illegal in combat**, so every
fight is to the death. The greed decision is therefore "do I open this door", never "do I finish
this fight" -- which is why the danger must be legible *before* the door.

Numbers and method: `docs/evidence/m4-attrition-sim.py`.
---

**RESOLVED 2026-09-10 — emberdelve-ffi.9 lifts the block on this ticket. What it constrains:**

Every room in the site that has fires carries a `fires { lit, to, moved }` object, and **at least
one room must move BRIGHTER** — or the brighter direction comes out of the design entirely. An
unexercised direction is AGENTS.md's measured "a capability flag is a claim, not a behaviour", and
this is the only site M4 has to exercise it in.

Why coverage matters: ~15 ALERT ticks across a delve against 6 segments is **2–3 fills**, each
moving whichever room the party is standing in. A room that cannot move wastes a fill. The site
walks twice — the entrance is the exit — so a room that goes dark on the way in is a room re-crossed
in the dark on the way out, which is where the dial actually pays.

The crypt is the DARKER example and is handled by emberdelve-4h9.16. The BRIGHTER one wants a
fiction that supports sconces being lit by something that has noticed you — the crypt's green fires
"that should have burned out centuries ago" are the wrong room for it.

title: Spend the kits - a prop appearance layer, not forty more PropTypes
description:
The kits on disk hold 145 GLBs - dungeon_props 48, ruins 92, characters 5. The game
uses six PropType values and ships five client scenes (DOOR came out of prop_table.tres
at the M3 playtest, because the wall hangs the door). Barrels, crates, chests, pots,
bookcases, tables, statues, cobwebs, skulls, banners, candles, bear traps, trapdoors and
spikes are all sitting there unused. The 4-5 room site is the reason to spend them.

THE TRAP TO AVOID

PropType is the enum ToolSchema builds the model's tool definitions from. Growing it
from six values to forty grows every schema the model reads every turn and hands it
forty things to hallucinate - and AGENTS.md already records that the tools model
hallucinates props. Section 9 says the way out: "props are handles, not depictions...
One generic container mesh does an enormous amount of work that way."

PROPOSED SHAPE - overrule this if you disagree, but decide it before authoring rooms

Separate what a prop MEANS from what it LOOKS LIKE.

  PropType stays small and mechanical. It answers: does this block a square, is it a
  container, is it a light source, is it a recess in a wall, is it scenery. Roughly
  today's six plus CONTAINER, STATUE, FURNITURE, REMAINS and a scenery catch-all.

  A new closed appearance field per type picks the mesh. CONTAINER covers Chest,
  Chest_Gold, Barrel, Barrel2, Crate, Pot1, Pot2, Pot3, Bag_Standing, Vase and Bucket -
  one type, eleven looks. STATUE covers Fox, Horse and Stag.

The tool schema names the type. reveal_prop and clicking both address props by id
anyway, so schema width stops growing with the kit while the room stops looking the same
twice.

THREE RULES THAT FALL OUT OF THAT

Appearance must never change blocking. PropType.blocksMovement is derived from the type
on purpose - the comment says a per-prop flag "would only be a chance to disagree with
the mesh". A CONTAINER blocks whether it is a chest or a barrel, or that reasoning is
gone.

The DM reads description, not the mesh name. The prop description field already carries
the specific look in prose. Appearance is a renderer concern and the seam is already
there.

The server ships appearance, the client never picks it (invariant 1). A client that
chose its own mesh would render a replayed session differently from the session.

THE PICKING HAZARD, AND IT IS NOT HYPOTHETICAL

From the 2026-09-06 playtest: "Only things you can act on are pick targets"... brazier-east,
"a 1x1 box around a narrow bowl, standing between the camera corner and the north wall -
won the ray, had no intent to offer, and fell through to a square that was null because
the ray had already left the room. The click did nothing and the failure was silent."

A room with twenty-five props is exactly where that comes back. Scenery must not shadow
a handle. And "a one-prop fixture will not find a picking bug" - test_overlay.gd's
DOORWAY fixture carries the crypt's furniture today and needs to carry a dense room.

HOUSEKEEPING

kits/crypt.json is the only kit manifest. ruins/ is an overgrown outdoor palette and is
most of where room-to-room variety will actually come from - a second manifest is
probably part of this.

kits/kaykit_dungeon/ and kits/kaykit_halloween/ hold zero GLBs. Find out whether they
are empty or unimported before assuming the inventory is 145.

Each kit keeps its own folder. Kit GLBs reference textures by relative path and mixing
two kits in one directory silently paints one with the other atlas (AGENTS.md,
Characters). ruins/ and dungeon_props/ are already separate; keep it that way.

Adding props is not a licence to retune lighting. The anti-goal timeboxes that and
emberdelve-27l already holds the one open lighting question.
acceptance_criteria:
A room renders around twenty props drawn from at least two kits and does not read as the
same room twice. The model's tool schema is no wider than it is today. Blocking is still
derived from PropType alone. test_overlay.gd holds a densely furnished room and turns red
if a scenery prop shadows the door or any other handle.
notes: CORRECTION 2026-09-07: the inventory figures in the description undercount. The original survey searched *.glb only, and two kits ship *.gltf. Real totals: dungeon_props 48 glb, ruins 92 glb, kaykit_dungeon 26 gltf, kaykit_halloween 15 gltf, characters 5 glb - 186 mesh files, not 145. kaykit_dungeon is not empty; it is the kit already in use, and room.gd names its floors, walls and torches directly. kaykit_halloween is 15 unused meshes and it is the most on-theme set on disk for this site: coffin, coffin_decorated, crypt, shrine, shrine_candles, plaque, plaque_candles, arch_gate, lantern_standing, pillar, skull, ribcage, bone_A/B/C. Note lantern_standing in particular - the 2026-09-06 playtest recorded that invented lanterns travel with the party as facts with no prop behind them, and there is a mesh for one.

title: A delve can end - extracted, empty-handed, or lost
description:
The gate is "does losing it sting", so a delve has to be losable and the loss has to
land. Section 9: "A delve can be lost, and losing it costs the run rather than a click."

Three endings at least: extracted with the objective, extracted without it, and lost.
Lost is a party wipe today because the party is one member; the shape should not assume
that.

There is prior art in this repo for the moment itself. From AGENTS.md, Since fixed:
"A dead player character used to be only a dropped token. Combat ended, the mode pill
flipped back to EXPLORATION, and nothing said what had happened - with the input box
refusing text and the board refusing clicks, that reads as a crash rather than a death."
The React Defeat screen solved it by marking the moment and offering the way on. That
screen predates the Godot migration; check what survived it. Either way the delve ending
needs the same treatment and more of it, because now there is a run to have lost rather
than a session to restart.

What makes it sting is what was spent, so the ending should say it: rooms entered,
potions drunk, what was carried, what was left behind. That is a read of state, not a
narration call, though a narration call over it is cheap and probably right.
acceptance_criteria:
Three endings reachable and distinguishable, each ending the delve as a state rather
than a screen. The client shows what was spent and what was carried out. Restarting is
one action and does not need the terminal.
notes:
SETTLED ON THE M4 MAP 2026-09-08 (emberdelve-ffi). Three amendments:

**`Ending` is descriptive, never a verdict.** `EXTRACTED_WITH_OBJECTIVE` / `EXTRACTED_WITHOUT` /
`PARTY_LOST`, not WON/LOST. §9's own first argument for bounded sites is that "a cleared site is a
durable fact" the campaign layer consumes; scoring the delve here pre-empts §10. The standing design
intent is that a bad outcome must never guarantee campaign failure — player creativity and DM
improvisation should be able to open another path — and an enum that judges takes that away.

**Only `PARTY_LOST` is losing.** Extracting empty-handed is a legitimate cautious outcome and
nothing should read as a scolding. §9's greed decision only works if leaving early is respectable;
punish the empty-handed exit and the site has one correct line through it.

**`DelveEnded` is an event.** Folded into `WorldState`, shipped in `SceneState`. Under invariant 8
there is no second write path, and the end of a delve is the single most important thing that
happens in a session — if it is not in the log it will not replay. `godot/chrome/defeat.gd`'s
client-side `hp <= 0` check on a hardcoded `"fighter"` goes: it cannot distinguish three endings and
it names a singleton player against invariant 2.

Death is no longer instant — 4h9.13 makes 0 hit points a downed clock. How the ending reads is
emberdelve-ffi.4.

title: The objective is an engine-owned prop, and the exit checks for it
description:
Section 9, Props are handles: "The objective is engine-owned, never narrator-asserted.
It is a prop with an id, taking it emits an event, and the exit checks for it. This is
the difference between an objective and a copper key."

The copper key is the reference failure and it is worth restating because this task is
the fix for it. The M2 gate produced a copper key found in a lamp's fat, asserted,
durable, and turning a lock in a door that still could not open (m2-evaluation.md
section 4). assert_fact made the DM consistent about it; nothing made the board agree.
An objective that lives in facts is another copper key. This one is a Prop with an id,
a take event, and a fold.

Depends on props being click targets. Routing "take the relic" through free text alone
puts a mechanical outcome back on the narrator's side of the governing principle —
section 2a says exactly this, and it is why the exits-only rule was reversed.

Section 9 also says where it sits: "the objective sits shallow and there is more worth
taking deeper, so the player can leave the moment they have what they came for. That is
tension for free, inside a bounded space, with an ending."

The exit checking for it is half the task. Leaving without the objective is legal and
means something different from leaving with it.
acceptance_criteria:
The objective is a Prop with an id in room content. Taking it emits an event that folds
into WorldState. The exit reads that state. A test takes it, leaves, and asserts the
delve ended carrying it; a second test leaves without it and asserts a different ending.
No fact and no narration is load-bearing in either path.

title: The Clock primitive, at DELVE scale
description:
Section 9, The delve clock: "Without pressure, go deeper costs nothing and the greed
decision is fake. A clock is the pressure."

Build the primitive from section 9 exactly, at DELVE scale only:

  record Clock(ClockId id, ClockScale scale, int filled, int segments,
               ClockKind kind, ConsequenceId consequence)

Three scales are named in the design (DELVE, WATCH, FRONT) and only DELVE is in scope.
The enum carries all three because the record is meant to be built once — section 9,
One primitive, three scales. Do not build the other two.

Ticks on rooms entered, rests taken, and noisy failures. When it fills it fires a table.
The table is the point: it is the same constrain-the-model pattern as the DC bands in
section 7 and the prop enum in section 5. The DM narrates what the table produced; it
never decides that the torch went out.

Consequences reach the prompt through the world-state projection (section 12), which
never truncates, so a filling clock is something the DM can foreshadow honestly. That is
the same reason the projection works at all: the DM cannot contradict a board that is in
front of it.
acceptance_criteria:
A Clock record with a tick event and a fold. At least two clocks running in a delve —
light and one of alert or wandering. Filling one fires a consequence from a table, not
from the model. The DM prompt shows clock state every turn. A scripted test fills a clock
and asserts the consequence, with no model in the path.
notes:
SETTLED ON THE M4 MAP 2026-09-08 (emberdelve-ffi). Three amendments to this ticket:

**Clocks speak twice, not once.** A threshold fires a SIGN; the fill fires the consequence. Signs
are §9's region-scale "spoor, smoke, tracks" brought to delve scale — engine-fired, table-driven,
narrated by the DM. Reason: a clock that speaks only when it fills is a jump scare, and one that
speaks every tick is a segment counter with extra steps. Blocked on emberdelve-ffi.2 for what is
actually on all four tables.

**Noisy failures are specified.** A failed check ticks the LIGHT clock one segment; a natural 1
ticks two. §9 already named noisy failures as a trigger. This is also the reconciliation of a real
play observation — the DM narrating a dropped lantern on a rolled 1 was the right beat reached the
wrong way, since the board stayed bright. Now the engine ticks, the table fires, and the DM narrates
a real event. The natural die is already special under invariant 5.

**The clock is diegetic and unlabelled.** No segment counter on screen. The LIGHT clock reads as a
shrinking radius (4h9.12); the ALERT clock's entire read is its signs. The projection lets the DM
foreshadow the alert clock honestly, which is 4h9.14's job.

Two more clocks now exist at DELVE scale beyond the two this ticket names: rest ticks every running
clock one segment (4h9.11), and downed is a short clock of its own (4h9.13). Segment counts are
emberdelve-ffi.6's answer. **The clock cannot kill directly** — its job is to make leaving
attractive, not to be a second health bar.

---

RESOLVED BY emberdelve-ffi.2 — 2026-09-09. The four tables are written out in that ticket's
resolution comment; this ticket is no longer blocked on them. What the build has to honour:

**The power budget, which is the load-bearing rule.** A consequence may only do what a tool can
already do — a named, pre-validated bundle of events that already have an `Event` + `Diff` pair
(`EntitySpawned`, `EntityMoved`, `PropRevealed`, `CombatStarted`) plus state the engine already
models as a scalar. **No effect language.** §15 already puts the effect interpreter with the
content milestone; reaching it through the back door of a consequence table is the same tax under
a different name.

**A sign is a consequence whose bundle is empty.** One enum (`ConsequenceId`), one firing path,
one directive mechanism. A sign table's entries having empty bundles is a validation rule, not a
type — a separate `SignId` was considered and refused.

**The sign table is a map from segment to `ConsequenceId`**, not a single named threshold, so a
clock can be quiet early and loud late. **Signs fire on crossing upward only and re-arm on the way
down** — otherwise spending a torch fires `LIGHT_GUTTERING` on the turn the player fixed the light.

**Tick triggers, final:** rooms entered and rests tick both clocks; a failed check ticks LIGHT
(natural 1, two); a fight starting ticks ALERT; **LIGHT filling ticks ALERT**. That last one is
declared on the tick side, never inside `LIGHT_OUT` — a clock that ticks a clock from inside a
consequence is the first step toward a state machine nobody can trace.

**Discharge is asymmetric.** ALERT resets to empty when it fills; LIGHT stays full until a `torch`
is spent. Light is a quantity you spend, alert is a state that discharges — and without the reset
ALERT's table is a one-shot.

**Two new events, forced by invariant 8.** `ClockTicked`, carrying the *resulting fill* rather
than having the fold count ticks; and `ConsequenceFired`, inert in the fold, emitted **alongside**
the bundled events rather than instead of them. A `ConsequenceFired` the fold expands via the
tables would make a content file part of replay correctness — edit a table after a session is
recorded and it replays differently. Same argument `Event.PartyMoved` makes for carrying its
landing square. Schema bump, so `./gradlew recordFixture` after.

**A draw is logged inside `ConsequenceFired`, not as a `RollResult`.** Not a die the player
watches; `isDramatic()` would gate it out anyway.

**Signs ride the latched directive rail** (`pendingArrival`'s, not `narrateCombat`'s), so they
cost no extra model call. Arrival and sign both go, sign appended, **one clause** — AGENTS.md's
measured finding is that writing more made the model more verbose. A sign latched during combat is
**dropped**, under the standing asymmetry rule.

**New build work this surfaces:**

- **Room lighting has no `Diff`.** `RoomView` carries `LightingPreset lighting` but nothing in the
  `Diff` union can change it after the scene is sent. `THE_DARK_CLOSES_IN` needs one.
- **`Disposition { HOSTILE, WARY }` on a spawn**, and the rule that combat follows from the
  disposition rather than from the spawn. `WARY` needs no new machinery — the creature is on the
  board, no combat started, and a player swing starts one via `start_combat`. Two values, not one:
  an unexercised seam is a claim, not a behaviour.
- `DRAWN_BY_THE_NOISE` wants emberdelve-4h9.9 (more than one hostile). Not a hard block — until
  4h9.9 lands the ALERT table draws from the other three entries.

---
**Segment counts and tick rules settled by emberdelve-ffi.6.**

- **LIGHT: 6 segments. ALERT: 6 segments.** Signs at 2 / 4 / 5, as emberdelve-ffi.2 wrote them.
- **A torch resets LIGHT to empty** (not "adds N segments"). With 2 starting torches that is an
  18-tick light budget, against a careful five-room delve's ~9 ticks and a greedy one's ~15.
- **Every room entry ticks, including a room already visited.** The lantern does not care that you
  have been here. This is load-bearing: it makes going one room deeper cost **two** segments, one
  in and one out, which is what turns depth from vaguely risky into computable. A revisit-free rule
  would make deep exploration free to undo and the greed decision fake.

**REVERSAL -- what ticks LIGHT off a die.** Charting settled "a failed check ticks one segment; a
natural 1 ticks two". That is withdrawn. **A natural 1 ticks LIGHT one segment; an ordinary failed
check ticks nothing.**

Measured in the recorded sessions: `session-m2-twenty-turns.jsonl` has 20 checks and **14
failures**; `session-m3-traversal.jsonl` has 11 checks and **2 failures**. Same game, same player --
a sevenfold difference in fill rate, because M2's DM reached for DC 15-25 and M3's for DC 5-10. A
clock fed by failed checks has its fill rate set by the narrator's taste in difficulty, which is
exactly what emberdelve-ffi.2 made LIGHT predictable to avoid, and it hands scarcity to the one
component §9 says must never own it.

The play observation that motivated the original rule survives whole: the dropped lantern on a 1 is
still an engine tick, a fired table and a narrated event. It lands once or twice a delve; the room
tick carries the pressure and is fully player-controlled.

Numbers and method: `docs/evidence/m4-attrition-sim.py`.
---

**OPEN AGAINST THIS TICKET 2026-09-10 — emberdelve-ffi.9.** The tables above were written when the
only thing LIGHT meant was the party's lantern and the only thing ALERT meant was a wandering
hostile. Two proposals now put both clocks on the room's own fires as well: LIGHT filling puts the
braziers out, ALERT filling lights the wall torches. If either lands, some entries here are saying
the same thing twice, and a fire going out is an event under invariant 8 rather than a table entry
the client acts on. Do not build these tables until emberdelve-ffi.9 is resolved.
---

**RESOLVED 2026-09-10 — emberdelve-ffi.9. The block above is lifted; these tables can be built.**
Read that ticket's resolution comment for the arithmetic; what changes here:

- **THE_DARK_CLOSES_IN comes off the ALERT table as a `ConsequenceId`.** A room's fires are no
  longer a drawn entry. Every ALERT fill moves the party's current room one step, unconditionally,
  in the direction that room's `fires.to` names — declared on the **fill** side, exactly as "LIGHT
  filling ticks ALERT" is declared on the tick side rather than buried inside LIGHT_OUT.
- **Its no-spawn slot survives as `IT_PASSES_BY`** — something came near and went on — an entry
  with an **empty bundle**, which this ticket's own "a sign is a consequence whose bundle is empty"
  already makes legal. Without it the table is three entries that all bring a creature, which is
  the shape ffi.2 refused by name.
- **The drawn table filters at draw** to entries that would change something. A
  `ConsequenceFired` logged for a consequence that did nothing is a log that lies about what
  happened — the same objection that got bundled-events-only refused.
- **`Event.RoomLightingChanged(at, roomId, from, to)`**, riding the schema bump this ticket already
  owed for `ClockTicked` and `ConsequenceFired`, so it costs no second refused-log. Plus the
  `Diff.RoomLightingChanged(roomId, lighting)` this ticket already had filed as "Room lighting has
  no Diff", and `WorldState.lightingIn(roomId)` folded, defaulting to the authored preset.
  `GameEngine.roomView()` stops reading `structure.lighting()` and reads the fold.
- **The move latches a one-clause directive** on the sign rail (`pendingArrival`'s, not
  `narrateCombat`'s). The directive says it just happened; the projection line (emberdelve-4h9.14)
  keeps it true afterwards.
- **Client, and it is not a wider guard.** `world.gd:126` rebuilds only on a `roomId` change and
  its comment says why widening that is dangerous. Targeted instead: rebuild the `Torches` group
  and re-apply `lighting.gd`. Both calls are already driven from outside in
  `godot/dev/light_shots.gd`. Re-entering a moved room later is a `roomId` change and picks the new
  lighting up through the ordinary full rebuild for free.

---

**emberdelve-ffi.3 surfaced 2026-09-10: the directive rail is single-slot and about to have five
writers. Fix it here, before the first sign is built against it.**

`DmService.java:114` is **`private String pendingArrival`** — one slot. `noteCrossing` writes it
(`:948`), `takePendingArrival` clears it (`:952`), and only a free-text prose phase consumes it.

Writers it is about to have:

1. the arrival line that exists today (`ARRIVAL_FIRST` / `ARRIVAL_RETURN`, `DmService.java:73`, `:81`);
2. LIGHT's signs at segments 2, 4 and 5 (`emberdelve-ffi.2`);
3. ALERT's signs (same);
4. the room-fire move directive (`emberdelve-ffi.9`);
5. a torch relight (`emberdelve-ffi.3`).

**Last write wins, silently.** A sign that gets overwritten is a clock that went quiet — the exact
failure `emberdelve-ffi.2` built a sign table to prevent, and it presents as the DM losing interest
rather than as a bug. `emberdelve-ffi.2` said signs "ride the latched directive rail and cost no model
call"; that rail cannot hold two.

**Provenance, stated straight: the stale-directive half was already on the tracker.**
`emberdelve-xgg.12` recorded a stale "you have come back" directive landing **16 seconds later on a
key-searching turn**, after two rapid crossings, and noted it "could be fixed on its own without
adding any narration". What `emberdelve-ffi.3` adds is that the slot is about to have five writers
instead of one, which turns a P4 annoyance into a dropped sign.

**The fix: an ordered list, drained in order**, replacing the single `String`. Where it is drained —
one prose call per crossing or one per directive, and how an arrival line and a sign arriving together
are ordered — is `emberdelve-ffi.10`'s decision, not this ticket's. This ticket owns making the rail
able to hold them at all.

Also settled by `emberdelve-ffi.3`: **the LIGHT clock's segments are what the client's light level is
read from**, level-triggered, while signs stay edge-triggered (fire on crossing upward, re-arm on the
way down). Spending a torch at `FAILING` puts the level straight back to `FULL` and fires nothing on
the way down. Two rules, deliberately different: a sign is an announcement, a level is a state. The
level mapping lives in `emberdelve-4h9.12`.

title: Consumables as a counter map, and one use_item tool
description:
Section 9, Attrition: "Consumables are a counter map, not an inventory.
Map<Consumable, Integer> on PartyMember over a closed enum — potion, torch, rope — and
one use_item tool. No item entities, no equipping, no weight, no UI beyond a count."

The reasoning is worth keeping in front of whoever builds this: "The instinct to build
inventory here drags in an item pipeline, a screen, and an enum that grows forever, in
service of three numbers." Section 16 has the re-entry condition for real inventory and
this is not it.

Healing is the scarce one. Section 9: the engine has to impose scarcity because the
narrator never will. "The model always says yes. That is not a prompt failure to be
tuned out; it is what a narrator trained to be agreeable does."

use_item is a mechanics-phase tool, not reconcile: a false positive spends a potion the
player still has, which is expensive. Same test as every other tool placement in
AGENTS.md, LLM tools.

Counts fold out of the log like everything else (invariant 8). A new event, not a field
somebody sets.
acceptance_criteria:
Consumable is a closed enum. PartyMember carries a counter map folded from an event.
use_item is in the mechanics tool set, validated server-side, rejected when the count is
zero. The chrome shows counts as text and nothing more. A potion at zero cannot be drunk
however the player phrases it.
notes:
SETTLED ON THE M4 MAP 2026-09-08 (emberdelve-ffi): the `torch` consumable refuels the LIGHT clock.

§9's enum was already potion / torch / rope, and this gives the torch a job: it links this counter
map to 4h9.3's clock and states the greed loop in one line — how deep you go is how many torches you
brought. It is also what keeps the light clock non-terminal, which emberdelve-ffi records as a
deliberate choice (a clock that cannot be refuelled is a race, and §9 wants a greed decision).

Counts are emberdelve-ffi.6's answer. See also 4h9.12, which builds the light the torch feeds.

---
**Numbers settled by emberdelve-ffi.6.**

- **A potion restores 8** hit points, on a bar of 20 -- two fifths.
- **The party starts with 2 potions and 2 torches.** No rope in the starting kit; the enum carries
  it, the site does not need it yet.

Chosen for legibility rather than balance, and the sim is explicit about why: across a whole delve
a 3-point rest and an 8-point rest differ by under 1.5%, because the fights dominate completely.
The potion is deliberately worth twice a rest (emberdelve-4h9.11) -- being visibly stronger than
the free option is what justifies it being finite.

Numbers and method: `docs/evidence/m4-attrition-sim.py`.

---

**emberdelve-ffi.3 resolved 2026-09-10: "no UI beyond a count" is amended, not breached.**

The consumables get **buttons**, on an exploration action bar, alongside rest.

**The principle, which is the door's and is already structural in `net.gd`: a button per player
action the DM does not adjudicate.** `moveTo`, `enterExit`, `attack` and `endTurn` are typed client
messages that reach the engine with no model in the path, because none of them is a question the DM
answers. A torch that resets a clock, a fixed 8-point potion and `emberdelve-4h9.11`'s fixed 4-point
rest are the same shape — no roll, no discretion. *Clicking a door and walking through is the honest
path*, and so is drinking a potion you already own.

This amends the rule rather than punching through it. **The anti-goal here is inventory** — "an item
pipeline, a screen, and an enum that grows forever" — and a button per entry of a closed enum §16 has
already frozen cannot grow. Rope gets no button, because it has no effect yet, and a button for a
thing that does nothing is AGENTS.md's measured "a capability flag is a claim, not a behaviour".

**`use_item` stays in the mechanics tool set.** Rejected: the button replacing the tool. The player
will type *"I drink a potion"* whatever buttons exist, and a DM that narrates drinking one while
nothing happens is the hotdog with a healing potion in it. The button is a **second path to the same
event**, exactly as `enterExit` coexists with `use_exit`.

**Where the bar lives.** A sibling of `combat_bar.gd`, which is already the combat action bar; this is
its exploration counterpart. **Not** an extension of `party_badge.gd` — that node is
`MOUSE_FILTER_IGNORE` throughout and its own comment says it holds no facts, so making it clickable
inverts what it is. Every button keys off `Table.awaiting_dm`, the lock `debug_bar.gd:41` and
`combat_bar.gd:255` already use, so they go dead while the DM is speaking like everything else.

**Exploration-only — a finding, not a scope call.** `docs/evidence/m4-attrition-sim.py:60`: `fight()`
is "one fight to the death" and heals nobody; every rest and potion in `delve()` happens between
rooms (lines 112-116). So `emberdelve-ffi.6`'s **45.7% survival at exactly 5 hit points** was measured
with **no in-combat healing in it**. A mid-fight potion does not merely need an action-economy rule §6
defers and the anti-goal forbids — it invalidates the tuning that made §9's gate sentence
arithmetically true.

**The torch button is refused at exactly zero segments**, where it would reset nothing; the button
greys. Spending at `LOW` wastes two segments and stays legal, because that is the greed decision. An
action offered that provably does nothing is a lie in the UI, and it would log a `use_item` that
changed nothing — `emberdelve-ffi.9`'s filter-at-draw rule one level up.

The torch's own object model is `emberdelve-4h9.12`. The carried torch is **never** a pick target
(`emberdelve-7m6`).

title: Prove party state is session-scoped, not room-scoped
description:
Section 9 lists this as the small refactor everything else in the delve depends on:
"Party state is session-scoped, not room-scoped. Today entities are built from room
content, which makes hit points implicitly reset at a room boundary. Rooms should
contribute their occupants and props and nothing else."

M3 appears to have already done most of it. GameEngine.java:73 spawns the party once
at the entrance from entrance.startPositions().party(), and crossExit emits PartyMoved
rather than respawning, so entities survive a crossing in WorldState.entities. That is
a reading of the code, not a measurement.

The job is to prove it and close whatever gap is left, because every other child of
this epic is built on the assumption. Attrition that silently resets at a door is the
whole milestone failing quietly.

Look specifically at: whether anything rebuilds an Entity from RoomDefinition after the
first spawn; whether a room a party returns to re-contributes its occupants (a goblin
left alive in the crypt must be the same goblin, at the same hit points, per the
2026-09-07 playtest); and whether hit points, revealed props and facts all cross
correctly in both directions.
acceptance_criteria:
A test that walks the party across a room boundary and back with damage taken in each
room, asserting hit points, position and revealed state survive both crossings. If any
of it already holds, the test is the deliverable and says so.
notes:
**Settled by emberdelve-ffi.6 — the fighter's max hit points move 12 -> 20.**

Not PC tuning for its own sake: it is the delve-length dial, and no other dial does that job. The
doubt window (the hit points where surviving the next room is 40-70%) is set by the *encounter*,
not by max hit points -- HP 20 and HP 24 against the same foes have the identical window. What max
HP buys is the bar *above* the window. At 12 the brute's window (4-10) is more than half the bar,
so the player is in coin-flip territory from the first fight and the delve has no early phase to
spend. At 20 they descend 20 -> 10 through survivable ground and then enter it.

One number in `content/entities/fighter.json`. `AGENTS.md`'s shortcuts table Fighter row becomes
untrue when this lands and must be updated in the same change.

Numbers and method: `docs/evidence/m4-attrition-sim.py`.

title: EnvTorchlit's 1.1 ambient is the suspect number, not EnvDim's 0.7
description:
RECORDED, NOT SCHEDULED. Read the anti-goal before opening this.

Playtest 2026-09-07. The traversal design predicted the ambient drift between the two viewing directions and accepted it as a cost: standing in the gallery puts the crypt under EnvDim (ambient_light_energy 0.7, world.tscn:23), standing in the crypt puts the gallery under EnvTorchlit (1.1, world.tscn:14). The worry was that the darker direction would read as a void.

Play inverted it. 0.7 was judged the better look, and the crypt is the room it was judged on. So the drift is not a cost to tolerate — if anything the brighter environment is the weak one.

Two readings of the observation, both pointing the same way, neither resolved:
- the crypt seen from the gallery at 0.7 beat the gallery seen from the crypt at 1.1; or
- the crypt at 0.7 beat the crypt at 1.1, which is how it looks when you are standing in it.
The second is the more interesting claim, because it says EnvTorchlit is too bright for the room it was tuned for.

AGENTS.md § Anti-goals: 'Do not tune lighting and post-processing for more than one evening. Timebox it. This is the single largest time sink in the project and it will consume as much as you give it.' One observation from one session is not a tuning session. This is filed so the observation is not lost, not so someone acts on it.
acceptance_criteria: If ever opened: timeboxed to one evening, and judged by looking at both rooms from all four camera corners, not by reading numbers.
notes:
PULLED INTO THE M4 MAP 2026-09-08, and rescoped from "recorded, not scheduled" to a prerequisite.

M4's light clock is read as a shrinking radius around a party-carried lantern (emberdelve-ffi,
Settled at charting). At ambient_light_energy 1.1 a shrinking radius will not read at all — the
environment lifts the surfaces the radius is supposed to be leaving. So the judgement the light
work depends on cannot be made until this number moves.

The scope is deliberately narrower than the description above. This is NOT the tuning session the
anti-goal warns about, and it must not become one:

  - change EnvTorchlit's ambient_light_energy (world.tscn:14) from 1.1 toward EnvDim's 0.7
  - stand in the crypt and look
  - keep the number that wins

The second reading in the description is the one being tested — that EnvTorchlit is too bright for
the room it was tuned for — and it is testable by standing in the crypt, which does not require the
gallery or a crossing.

Blocks the light-radius prototype (emberdelve-ffi.5). Nothing else in the map waits on it.
close_reason: Resolved: EnvTorchlit ambient_light_energy 1.1 -> 0.7. See resolution comment.

comments.author: hampton.black
comments.text:
RESOLVED 2026-09-10. EnvTorchlit's ambient_light_energy goes 1.1 -> 0.7 (world.tscn:14).
preview_room.gd:194 restates the number and was moved with it; its own comment already says the
copy is a spike and 4h9.10 should read the environment off world.tscn instead.

HOW IT WAS JUDGED

Not by reading numbers. godot/dev/light_shots.gd renders the crypt through the real client --
world.tscn instantiated, Table fed a scene built from the real crypt.json, lighting.gd picking the
environment, room.gd building the torches, CameraRig at its own four corners -- and writes one
contact sheet per corner. No server, no key, no played session. Roderick stands at (10,10), away
from both braziers, because AGENTS.md is explicit that tokens carry a faint emissive of their own
albedo and that is what makes a darker ambient survivable: judging the light on an empty floor
judges the wrong picture.

THE COMPARISON THE TICKET RESTS ON HAD TWO VARIABLES IN IT, NOT ONE

The observation was "the crypt seen from the gallery at 0.7 beat the crypt stood in at 1.1". Those
two pictures differ by more than the ambient: room.gd only burns the torches of the room the party
is in, so the crypt seen from the gallery has its wall fires out. The braziers are props and stay
lit either way. So the sheets cross both axes, and the fires axis dominates completely.

WHAT THE AMBIENT ACTUALLY DOES

It does not light the floor. The torch pools own the floor at every value tried, down to 0.35.
What 1.1 buys is a blue-violet wash on the wall margins -- effective ambient is colour x energy, so
(0.235, 0.227, 0.322) x 1.1 = (0.26, 0.25, 0.35), a third bluer than it is red. At 1.10 the near
walls sit cool grey-blue against the torchlight; at 0.70 they read as dark stone and the fires
carry the picture. Both readings in the description pointed this way and the render agrees with
them once the fires are held still.

This confirms the Notes' operational claim precisely: the surfaces 1.1 lifts are the ones outside
the pools, which is the whole of what a shrinking light radius has to work with.

0.70 STILL BEATS 1.10 WITH THE FIRES OUT

Tested, not assumed. Lowering the ambient survives the change below.

IT DOES NOT COLLAPSE TORCHLIT INTO DIM

EnvDim's ambient colour is darker too, so at equal energy TORCHLIT still sits 1.67x above it
((0.235,0.227,0.322)x0.7 against (0.141,0.133,0.184)x0.7). A room you have left stays dimmer than
the room you are in, by colour rather than by energy -- arguably the more honest way for the two to
differ, and the M3 traversal design's predicted ambient drift between viewing directions is now
much smaller than the cost it was accepted as.

CARRIED FORWARD -- 0.70 IS SCOPED TO A TORCHLIT ROOM

Because 0.70 still shows the whole room's layout, a shrinking radius will change where the warm
light is, not what you can see. If the delve wants darkness to hide the room, the ambient has to go
well below 0.7 -- EnvDark's 0.35 territory. So this is the right answer for a torchlit room and
probably the wrong one for a delve room where the lantern is the only light. That is
emberdelve-ffi.5's problem and it is now a sharper question than it was.

WHAT THE SHEETS TURNED UP THAT THIS TICKET DID NOT ASK

The crypt looks better with the wall fires out altogether, and that is not a taste call: it is what
both recorded sessions have been describing. Filed as emberdelve-fmn (the build) and
emberdelve-ffi.9 (the decision the LIGHT and ALERT tables now have to make). Neither is this
ticket's to resolve.

The harness is kept rather than deleted. emberdelve-ffi.5 needs exactly this, and the anti-goal's
one-evening timebox is only affordable if looking at the room costs minutes.

Godot suite: 246/246 pass after the change. Nothing in server/ moved.

title: A click crossing narrates nothing, and arms a stale arrival directive
description:
RECORDED, NOT SCHEDULED. Play says this is fine — see the note at the end before working on it.

WsHandler.enterExit (WsHandler.java:118) sends the new Scene, calls dm.noteCrossing, and stops. noteCrossing arms pendingArrival, but DmService.takePendingArrival (DmService.java:934) is only consumed by a free-text prose phase, which the click path never runs. So crossing by clicking the door produces no narration at all.

Playtest 2026-09-07: 15 of 17 crossings across the two sessions were silent. Only the two typed ones ('I go through the doorway', 'I enter the doorway') got an arrival line.

Secondary, and the part that is arguably wrong regardless: the armed directive is not discarded. It waits and attaches to whatever the player types next, which may be several crossings later. Session 2 clicked gallery->crypt->gallery at 19:59:27 and 19:59:30; the stale 'you have come back' directive landed on a key-searching turn 16 seconds afterwards. Repeated clicks also push a threshold marker into history each time with no reply between them.

WHY THIS IS P4. The DmService.pendingArrival javadoc says the silence is deliberate. The player who ran both sessions confirmed it did not bother them: clicking a door and walking through is the honest path, and narrating it is not what was missing. What was missing was knowing whether the door could be crossed at all — that is emberdelve-xgg.10, now fixed.

If it is ever wanted, it is small: a narrateArrival(TurnSink) modelled on openScene (DmService.java:177) with takePendingArrival() as the directive and tryLock rather than lock, plus one submit in enterExit. turnSink(ctx) already exists. The stale-directive half could be fixed on its own without adding any narration.

title: Turn-1 escalation is a coin flip
description:
Playtest 2026-09-07. Two sessions opened with the identical move — 'I inspect the sarcophagus', failed INVESTIGATION, the first check of the session — and produced two different games.

Session 1 (20260907-030629): spawn_entity only. Five turns of parley followed, and the fight started later when the player chose it.
Session 2 (20260907-195254): spawn_entity AND start_combat in the same response, 4s apart. In initiative before the player had done anything hostile.

dm-tools.md:47 says the situation must change on the SECOND consecutive failure. Both runs escalated on the first failure of the session, and read the same rule opposite ways.

This is the M2 finding 'talking to yourself can start a fight' in a new form, and it is not cosmetic: it decides whether the player gets a negotiation or a fight, on turn one, before they have any information.

The Momentum block only appears when consecutiveFailedChecks > 0 (DmService.java:833), so on the first failure of a session the model sees no momentum line at all and escalates anyway.
acceptance_criteria: A single failed check on turn 1 does not start combat. The two-failure rule holds across repeated runs of the same opening — check it by replaying, not by reading the prompt.
notes:
Blocks emberdelve-4h9.5 as of 2026-09-07. Left standalone rather than pulled into M4, but it stops being cosmetic there: an attrition game whose first fight is decided by a coin flip on turn one is unfair in a way the current no-stakes game hides.

DECIDED ON THE M4 MAP by emberdelve-ffi.2 — 2026-09-09. Not yet built; this ticket is now an
implementation, not an open question.

**`start_combat` stays, for provoked fights. `dm-tools.md`'s two-failure escalation rule goes.**
The engine's ALERT clock becomes the only source of an *unprovoked* fight.

What was wrong was never that the model could start a fight — a player who swings a sword needs
one to start, and routing that through a clock is absurd. What was wrong is that *unprovoked*
escalation was decided by a model reading a rule it reads two ways. Both 2026-09-07 sessions
escalated on the **first** consecutive failure, against a rule that says the second; one then put
the player in initiative before they had done anything hostile. That rule was not producing
tension, it was producing a coin flip, and it decides what kind of game the session is on turn one.

The replacement is a clock the player has been given signs about: ALERT ticks on rooms entered,
rests, and fights starting, speaks at thresholds, and fires a table when it fills. Escalation
becomes something the player can read coming and act on, which is what the rule was reaching for.

**The behavioural change, named rather than left to be found in play:** ALERT does not tick on
failed checks (that is LIGHT's trigger). So a player who fails check after check in one room now
generates no escalation at all, where today they would get a fight. That is intended — failed
checks still cost, in the currency that does not ambush you — but it is a real change to a
milestone that passed its gate, and the M4 gate session (emberdelve-4h9.15) should watch for it.

`## Momentum` keeps its count regardless: emberdelve-ffi.1 settled that a count driving a tool
decision stays a count, and momentum is still a fact the narrator should have even once it stops
gating an escalation rule.

title: Play the dungeon and decide whether DIM reads
description:
The gate for this epic. Everything else in it is decided by a fixture; this is
decided by looking.

Must be played in the real Godot client, not headless. AGENTS.md still carries
"Dark neighbour unread" from the M3 gate for exactly this reason — that session
was headless, so whether a room through a doorway reads as a dungeon or as a
hole has never actually been judged.

Follow the M3 gate's shape: cross at least four times, spend real turns in each
room, and rotate the camera (Q/E) through all four corners in both rooms.

WHAT TO LOOK AT

1. The complaint. Does crossing still read as a cut to a new box, or as walking
   into the next part of one place?
2. The crypt's north corners, seen from the gallery, from ALL FOUR camera
   corners. This is the xgg.7 verification and the whole reason the wall rule
   was rewritten. A wall can be right from three corners and wrong from the
   fourth.
3. DIM in both directions, and compare them. The crypt seen from the gallery is
   lit by ambient 0.7; the gallery seen from the crypt by ambient 1.1. That
   drift is predicted and accepted (ADR-0010 era decision, Q9 of the design) —
   the question is whether the darker direction still reads as somewhere you
   have been rather than as a void.
4. Props across a crossing. Reveal the crypt's alcove, cross, look back: still
   there? Reveal the gallery's niche, cross twice: still there? This is
   traversal itself plus the room-qualified PropRef.
5. The camera in the gallery, whose origin is not (0,0). Does the clamp fight
   the follow? Then `debug -> start combat` there: does the framing centre on
   the gallery or snap back toward the crypt?
6. Picking. A click in the DIM room does nothing and swallows no move; the door
   back is still clickable; brazier-east still does not shadow the door.
7. A goblin left behind. Spawn one in the crypt, cross to the gallery, look
   back. The crypt should show no token — ADR-0011's accepted cost. Confirm it
   reads as absence rather than as a bug.
8. The DM, asked about a room it is not in. Type something like "I look back
   through the door at the crypt" and see whether the narration stays coherent
   without the prompt having been widened.
design:
The one decision this session exists to make: DIM or LIT for visited rooms.

That was chosen as DIM in the design grilling with LIT named as the fallback,
and Room.level_for was built to keep the switch to one line. If the darker
direction reads as a void, pull it. If it reads as a room you have been in,
leave it. Either answer closes this ticket; "it was fine" without having looked
at both directions does not.

Two other outcomes ride on this session:

- ADR-0011 is Proposed, not Accepted. It flips to Accepted if item 6 holds in
  play — that is the picking confinement being exercised rather than merely
  compiled.
- If the ambient drift is the problem rather than DIM itself, the second knob is
  a per-room tint, not a change of level. Recorded in the epic's design so the
  fix is not reinvented as "raise the ambient", which AGENTS.md already warns
  against for a different reason.

The session writes itself to server/sessions/. If anything goes wrong, the file
that proves it is already on disk — copy it into docs/evidence/ and it replays
on every build. That is the M2 workflow and it is the reason this ticket does
not need a reproduction script.
acceptance_criteria:
- Four or more crossings played in the real client, camera rotated through all
  four corners in both rooms.
- No hole at the crypt's north corners from any camera corner.
- A written verdict on DIM vs LIT, having looked at both directions, and the
  one-line change made if the verdict is LIT.
- ADR-0011 moved from Proposed to Accepted, or a note saying why not.
- Any fault found is filed with its session file, copied into docs/evidence/ if
  it is worth replaying.
notes:
Item 4 was not actually exercised by the 2026-09-07 sessions. Session 1 revealed zero props. Session 2 revealed the crypt alcove at 20:04:57, after the last crossing at 20:04:24 — so no prop was ever revealed and then crossed away from and returned to. The gallery niche was never found in either run: the player searched the brazier and the pillars, and the revealHint is on the west wall. 'Props survive a crossing' and the room-qualified PropRef are still untested in play.

Everything else on the list was covered, and the epic's DIM question was answered by looking.
close_reason: Played in the real client over two sessions on 2026-09-07. DIM stands — the fallback to LIT is not taken, and the darker direction was judged the better look, inverting the design's expectation that the drift was a cost. ADR-0011 flips to Accepted: picking confinement held in play, and the goblin left behind read as absence rather than as a bug. Findings recorded in AGENTS.md § Judged in play — playtest 2026-09-07. Item 4 (a prop revealed and then crossed away from) was not exercised and is noted there rather than left implied.

title: Draw the shared wall the way coveredWalls() decides it
description:
Rooms.coveredWalls() holds the shared-wall rule server-side, with tests, since emberdelve-5sc: the plane is owned by whichever room is nearer the entrance (ties by roomId), and omission is a 1D interval overlap rather than a direction match. Nothing ships it. RoomView carries no covered-segment field, so room.gd still omits by direction — the room the party is standing in draws the plane, every other room drops the whole run its answering door is in.

Two consequences on screen: the crypt's two 1-unit corner overhangs are missing when seen from the gallery (a hole in a wall is a way out), and with more than two rooms drawn the ownership flips with the party rather than staying put.

Wire it: add the covered segments to RoomView (or a per-room list on SceneState), have GameEngine.scene() fill it from Rooms.coveredWalls(), and have Room._build_walls skip exactly those segments instead of whole runs. Room.build already takes a RoomView and is the one build path for every room, current or not, so this is the last piece.
design: Deliberately left out of emberdelve-xgg.4, which delivered the render levels, the persistent world frame on the client and per-room prop holders. Wiring coveredWalls() is a wire change plus a client rule swap, and it is testable on its own — the synthetic three-room chain in RoomsTest already proves the server half.
acceptance_criteria:
A neighbour drawn beside the current room keeps the part of its perimeter that overhangs the shared run: no hole at the crypt's north corners seen from the gallery.
No two rooms draw stone on the same plane (the seam does not go to noise, and no door grows a second ring handle).
Ownership does not change when the party crosses: the same room draws the same plane from either side.
AGENTS.md's 'decided server-side and not yet drawn' bullet is replaced by what is drawn.
notes: Second hole the whole-run omission leaves, found reviewing emberdelve-xgg.4: with three rooms drawn, a shared plane can be drawn by nobody. omit_shared_wall is now 'every room but the one the party is in', and _on_a_shared_wall drops the run by direction — so in A(current)-B-C, B and C both omit their mutual run and the wall between them is missing entirely. Latent while M3 ships two rooms; live the day a third exists. coveredWalls() already gets this right (exactly one room owns each plane).
close_reason: RoomView.coveredWalls ships Rooms.coveredWalls()' answer and room.gd omits exactly those segments — the crypt's north corners are stone from the gallery, every plane is drawn once by the same room from either side, and the A-B-C plane two neighbours both used to drop is drawn. The doorway is the deliberate exception: a door is one object two rooms address by two ids and World._target_under only scans the current room's walls, so the room the party is in hangs it and every other room leaves its openings open. Room.build takes the current room id rather than a Level so that the agreed DIM-to-LIT fallback cannot hang a second door. Five TDD'd tests, all three client ones mutation-checked against the old direction-match rule. AGENTS.md, ADR-0010 and CONTEXT.md amended. Filed emberdelve-xgg.9 for the generator-era case where a covering room is not on the wire.

title: Record the world-frame decisions and fix the docs they contradict
description:
Written after the server half proves itself, before the client half is wired.

- docs/adr/0009: the world frame is server-owned and anchored at the entrance;
  a shared wall is owned by BFS distance and omitted by geometric overlap;
  visible is not addressable. One ADR, because they are one decision about where
  world-space authority lives.
- CONTEXT.md: add "world frame" and "render level"; correct "scene state", which
  currently reads "the client's whole current picture of a room" and is no longer
  true. Flag any term the code needs that the glossary lacks.
- AGENTS.md's shared-wall bullet is NOT amended here — it goes in emberdelve-5sc,
  in the same commit that makes it false.
design:
Deliberately not written up front. This repo's docs are empirical — AGENTS.md is
wall-to-wall "measured" and "found in play", and ADR-0008 is literally "model
picks come from played sessions". An ADR written before implementation is a
prediction, and the interval-overlap wall rule is the piece most likely to come
back different. Writing it once the synthetic three-room fixture proves the world
frame and the wall rule means it records something demonstrated, while still
landing early enough that the client is built against a written-down rule.

Glossary entries land with the code introducing each term, not in a batch.
acceptance_criteria:
- ADR-0009 exists, follows docs/adr/0000-template.md, and states what was
  rejected (client-side offset accumulation; full world-space packing) and why.
- CONTEXT.md's "scene state" entry is true of the shipped SceneState.
- No rule in AGENTS.md or CONTEXT.md contradicts the code after this epic closes.
